clue.text: Sea-dweller born after channel island turned almost arctic

indicators.note: after says the piece for born comes behind the rest

parts.note: Herm is one of the smaller Channel Islands, near Guernsey

indicators.note: turned tells us the shortened word is to be read backwards
almost means the word arctic loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A sea creature is born after an island in the English Channel turned nearly arctic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ARCTIC to ARCTI and 'turned' reverses it to ITCRA; 'after' puts B behind HERM + ITCRA. Herm is one of the Channel Islands between England and France.
explanation.definitionFit: This crustacean lives in the sea, sheltering in borrowed shells, so it is a marine creature.

clue.text: Kick of a horse

definitions.meaning: to kick an opponent's shins, as in rugby
a riding horse for hire or ordinary riding

explanation.surface: A horse lashing out with its hoof.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to kick at the shins; as a noun, an ordinary riding horse.

clue.text: Venetian general up in space

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Othello, the Moor of Venice, was a general in the Venetian service

explanation.surface: A Venetian commander rises into outer space.
explanation.walkthrough: Othello is the Moor; 'up' reverses it in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Room means capacity or area to move in.

clue.text: Putting everything in, in position

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a station is a position or post

explanation.surface: Setting up a machine, with every part put in its proper place.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' puts ALL inside STATION; the second 'in' is the letters IN at the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The act of setting something in place, such as equipment, is fitting or putting it in.

clue.text: "If thy heart fails thee, — not at all", the Queen advised Ralegh

definitions.text: If thy heart fails thee, — not at all", the Queen advised Ralegh

parts.words: If thy heart fails thee, — not at all", the Queen advised Ralegh
parts.note: Elizabeth I's reply to a line Sir Walter Ralegh scratched on a window, fearing to rise for fear of falling

explanation.surface: Queen Elizabeth's famous advice to her courtier.
explanation.walkthrough: Ralegh wrote 'Fain would I ... yet fear I to fall'; the Queen wrote beneath it the line in the clue, with the same missing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing verb means to ascend or rise, here in royal favour.

clue.text: Music-maker's agreement upset no one

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, linking the definition to the wordplay

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the pieces are turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A musician's contract is overturned with nobody in favour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns NO + I into ION, following ACCORD.
explanation.definitionFit: A squeezebox played with bellows and buttons is an instrument, something that produces music.

clue.text: Record, one about heroes

parts.note: an EP is an extended-play record
I is the Roman numeral for one
c. (circa) is the abbreviation for about

explanation.surface: A record or account that tells of heroic deeds.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a long heroic poem, while also giving EP, I and C in turn.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrative poem recounting heroic deeds is precisely a record of heroes.

clue.text: Leaves to contain crime in homes like the Brontes'

indicators.note: to contain means the pages wrap around the crime

parts.note: leaves of a book are pages

explanation.surface: Autumn foliage enclosing a criminal act in Victorian houses.
explanation.walkthrough: The Brontë sisters grew up in the house of their clergyman father at Haworth.
explanation.definitionFit: A vicar's residence, like the one at Haworth where the Brontës lived, is a clergy house.

clue.text: Peninsula contains cheese ? About right, my lad

indicators.note: about means the word cheese goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a son is a lad, as a father might say my lad

explanation.surface: A headland apparently made of dairy produce, as a father tells his boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' is only a link; 'About' wraps CHEESE around R + SON.
explanation.definitionFit: This Greek-derived word names a peninsula, as in the Thracian or Tauric one.

clue.text: Horizontal member appears a bit annoyed

explanation.surface: Someone seems slightly irritated, with a hint of a club or committee member.
explanation.definitionFit: A transverse bar or beam in a structure is a horizontal structural member.

clue.text: Famous huntsman's faithful hound

parts.note: the song D'ye Ken John Peel lists his hounds Ranter, Ringwood, Bellman and one more whose name also means faithful

explanation.surface: A celebrated hunter's loyal dog.
explanation.walkthrough: John Peel was a Cumbrian huntsman celebrated in an English folk song naming his hounds; the last of them shares its name with a word for loyal.
explanation.definitionFit: The hound in the John Peel song bears a name meaning loyal or faithful.

clue.text: The preacher who followed proverbs

definitions.meaning: the Hebrew title Qoheleth is rendered as The Preacher
the Old Testament book that comes after Proverbs

explanation.surface: A clergyman who obeyed wise sayings.
explanation.definitionFit: This Old Testament book, placed after Proverbs, is attributed to Qoheleth, the Preacher.

clue.text: Scene of a musical ride

parts.note: the nursery rhyme Ride a Cock-Horse sends the rider to a place in Oxfordshire, where she has bells on her toes and makes music wherever she goes

explanation.surface: Where a ride with music takes place.
explanation.walkthrough: The English nursery rhyme 'Ride a cock-horse to ...' tells of a fine lady with rings on her fingers and bells on her toes, so the ride is musical.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oxfordshire market cross is the destination of the rhyme's tinkling horseback journey.

clue.text: Comic PC fuddled with ale from partner in crime

indicators.note: fuddled, as if drunk, means the letters are mixed up

explanation.surface: A funny policeman befuddled by beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'from' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who helps another commit an offence is an associate in wrongdoing.

clue.text: Love rises in man not heartlessly spiteful

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside the other
rises in a down clue means the word is read upwards
heartlessly means the middle letter of the word not is removed

explanation.surface: Affection grows in a man who is spiteful without heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rises' turns LOVE into EVOL, which goes 'in' MALE; 'heartlessly' cuts NOT to NT.
explanation.definitionFit: Wishing harm to others is the same as being malicious.

clue.text: Take tea with the king of France in Belgium

parts.note: char is British slang for tea
le roi is French for the king

explanation.surface: Having tea with the French monarch while in Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is just a link here. CHAR is everyday British slang for a cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: This industrial city lies in the Hainaut province of southern Belgium.

clue.text: Blue after battering ? But allegation is this

indicators.note: battering suggests the letters are beaten into a new shape

explanation.surface: Bruised after a beating, but the claim can be challenged.
explanation.definitionFit: An allegation that can be disproved is open to rebuttal.

clue.text: What scholars do with King, and no lost love

indicators.note: lost means the letter for love goes missing from the word no

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, so O

explanation.surface: Academics' activity, done with a monarch and with no lost affection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lost' takes O (love, zero in tennis scoring) out of NO, leaving N to follow LEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Scholars study and acquire knowledge, which is to say they acquire understanding.

clue.text: Round, green, open

explanation.surface: A list of three adjectives describing perhaps a golf course.
explanation.walkthrough: VERT is the heraldic word for green.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done in plain view, not hidden, is public or unconcealed.

clue.text: Jeremy's holding in those completing the course

indicators.note: holding means one piece clasps the other inside it

parts.note: Jeremy Fisher is the frog in Beatrix Potter's tale, so Jeremy's is Fisher's

explanation.surface: A man named Jeremy hangs on among the people who complete a race.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Fisher is the frog in a Beatrix Potter children's story; 'holding' puts IN inside FISHERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Runners who reach the end of a race course have finished it.

clue.text: Describes perhaps part poor lion had as his share

definitions.text: Describes perhaps part poor lion had as his share

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of the following words could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: A fable about a poor lion and the portion he received.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals the anagram of PART POOR LION. The whole clue doubles as the meaning: a share in measure with one's part, ironic given the proverbial lion's share.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjective for a portion matching one's contribution, a share in correct relation to the whole.

clue.text: Bursting out of one's robe, see!

definitions.text: Bursting out of one's robe, see!

indicators.note: out of tells us the letters come from within the words robe, see

explanation.surface: Someone is too large for their gown.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is found within 'robe, see', and the whole clue describes someone too fat for their clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone so fat they are splitting their gown is grossly overweight.

clue.text: Growing boy from both ends of 1 ac

indicators.note: from both ends of means only the opening and closing letters of 1 across are kept

explanation.surface: A lad who is getting bigger.
explanation.walkthrough: Keep the start and finish of 1 across, dropping its middle. The definition plays on a plant that grows and a boy's short name, short for Herbert.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant grows, and it is also a boy's name shortened from Herbert.

clue.text: Tempest scene one found noisy

parts.note: Caliban in Shakespeare's The Tempest says his island home is full of noises

explanation.surface: A stage setting in Shakespeare that someone found loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Caliban's speech begins 'Be not afeard; the ... is full of noises', so the setting is noisy.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tempest is set on a remote island, which Caliban says is full of noises.

clue.text: Animal that's seen round Beachy Head an unknown quantity

indicators.note: round means the other letters go around the piece from Beachy
Head picks the first letter of Beachy

explanation.surface: A creature spotted near a famous Sussex headland, an unknown amount of it.
explanation.walkthrough: Beachy Head is a chalk headland on the English south coast, but here 'Head' just takes its first letter B, which IE + X go 'round'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wild mountain goat of the Alps is an animal.

clue.text: Intransitive thing minus or without purpose

explanation.surface: A grammatical verb is described as missing a thing or being aimless.
explanation.walkthrough: A second definition, 'without purpose', follows after 'or': the word also means aimless.
explanation.definitionFit: An intransitive verb takes no direct object, so it is without one.

clue.text: Invested in this Italian house

indicators.note: in tells us the letters are found inside the word Invested

explanation.surface: Money put into a noble Italian dynasty.
explanation.walkthrough: The house of Este was a ruling family of Ferrara and Modena.
explanation.definitionFit: The Este family were a noble dynasty ruling Ferrara, so an Italian ducal house.

clue.text: Strange Sea-bed Life. This title could be cancelled:

indicators.note: strange suggests the letters of the following words are put in an odd order

explanation.surface: Odd marine life is noted, and a title might be revoked.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal term for a right or title capable of being annulled or made void.
